pr_title: Fix hang in HTTP/2 handling of canceling credit waits
pr_comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/ncl
See info in area-owners.md if you want to be subscribed.

> How can this be tested?

I validated it with your repro.

> Should a new HTTP/2 stress test be added?

Ideally, yes. There are many corner cases the stress suite should cover; it's very limited right now.

I'm probably missing something, but why can't you do something similar to the cancellation logic in the write queue? https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/Http2Connection.cs#L797

That is:
(1) Just do a simple cancellation registration that cancels the task
(2) Before calling task.SetResult, dispose the cancellation registration and check if the task was actually cancelled. If so, do nothing; if not, you're now guaranteed it won't be cancelled and it's safe to call SetResult

Test failures seem related:
```
System.Net.Http.Functional.Tests: [Long Running Test] 'System.Net.Http.Functional.Tests.SocketsHttpHandlerTest_Http2.PostAsyncNonDuplex_ServerCompletesResponseBodyThenResetsStreamWithNoError_SuccessAndRequestBodyCancelled', Elapsed: 00:02:00
```
i.e.: `PostAsyncNonDuplex_ServerCompletesResponseBodyThenResetsStreamWithNoError_SuccessAndRequestBodyCancelled` test hangs.

> why can't you do something similar to the cancellation logic in the write queue?

It is similar.  It can't do the exact same thing because it's not a TaskCompletionSource / Task here.  TCS has built-in synchronization via CompareExchange operations to guarantee that the Task is only transitioned to completed by one thread. ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore has no such built-in synchronization, so this PR is effectively layering that on top.

> It is similar. It can't do the exact same thing because it's not a TaskCompletionSource / Task here. TCS has built-in synchronization via CompareExchange operations to guarantee that the Task is only transitioned to completed by one thread. ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore has no such built-in synchronization, so this PR is effectively layering that on top.

Okay, but I don't think the approach I described actually relies on the TCS completion synchronization you mentioned. Am I missing something?

> Am I missing something?

TCS isn't reusable: once canceled, always canceled.  With the reusable credit waiter, the moment it transitions to a completed state, whoever was waiting for that can wake up and continue processing, which could in turn cause it to come back around for the next operation that would reuse/reset the instance.  If that all happened fast enough, the code doing the "dispose cancellation then check" could see the "task" as not being canceled and try to complete it, even if it had actually been canceled and then reset.  Now, maybe by construction the way the credit waiter is used in all cases ensures that can't happen?  I've not examined all such code paths.

> If that all happened fast enough, the code doing the "dispose cancellation then check" could see the "task" as not being canceled and try to complete it, even if it had actually been canceled and then reset

Yep, makes sense.

It seems like this could be dealt with by having a way to atomically dispose the cancellation registration and check whether it was actually cancelled.

But since we don't have that, we need to do some sort of coordination here.

> > Am I missing something?
> 
> TCS isn't reusable: once canceled, always canceled. With the reusable credit waiter, the moment it transitions to a completed state, whoever was waiting for that can wake up and continue processing, which could in turn cause it to come back around for the next operation that would reuse/reset the instance. If that all happened fast enough, the code doing the "dispose cancellation then check" could see the "task" as not being canceled and try to complete it, even if it had actually been canceled and then reset. Now, maybe by construction the way the credit waiter is used in all cases ensures that can't happen? I've not examined all such code paths.

I can confirm that there is at least one case where `CreditWater` is re-used and can transit from reset to pending state several time. It's in [Http2Stream.SendDataAsync](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6bb251ed2e57aabe6879a2da0aa72f5872259906/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/Http2Stream.cs#L1103).

> It seems like this could be dealt with by having a way to atomically dispose the cancellation registration and check whether it was actually cancelled.
> 
> But since we don't have that, we need to do some sort of coordination here.

That said, I notice that Unregister does in fact return a bool that according to MSDN is "true if the method succeeds; otherwise, false."

Does this mean that true == not cancelled and false == cancelled? If so, seems like we could use this to do the necessary coordination...

> Does this mean that true == not cancelled and false == cancelled? If so, seems like we could use this to do the necessary coordination...

Potentially, but it'd require some more effort and storing more state and I'm not sure it'd be better.  The two related problems are if:
a) a default CancellationToken is passed in
b) the non-default CancellationToken has cancellation requested prior to UnsafeRegister being invoked
In both cases, _registration will end up being a default registration, such that Unregister will return false.  The code paths using that to determine whether to call SetResult would need to differentiate those cases from ones where it got back false because the callback is/was invoked.

I don't quite follow. 

Just to help me out, what does the return value from Unregister mean, exactly? Am I correct in assuming that true == not cancelled and false == cancelled, or is this wrong? Does it somehow depend on whether the CancellationToken was cancelled at the time of registration? (in which case the return value is determined by a race, and therefore meaningless?)

> Am I correct in assuming that true == not cancelled and false == cancelled

No. It returns true if the registration represents an actual registration and it successfully removes it. It returns false otherwise. So, for example, if you do `default(CT).Register(...).Unregister()`, that returns false because the Register on the default CT doesn't actually register anything because the token won't ever be canceled / isn't backed by a CTS. Similarly, ct.Register on an already canceled token returns a dummy registration, on which Unregister will return false.

I think I understand, thanks.

Given this I don't see any way to simplify the logic here, so I'll stop making suggestions along those lines :)
@stephentoub Are you going to add something else to this PR or I can merge it? As I said above it's LGTM.

>  It returns true if the registration represents an actual registration and it successfully removes it. It returns false otherwise. So, for example, if you do default(CT).Register(...).Unregister(), that returns false because the Register on the default CT doesn't actually register anything because the token won't ever be canceled / isn't backed by a CTS. Similarly, ct.Register on an already canceled token returns a dummy registration, on which Unregister will return false.

Thinking about this more...

It seems like there are three cases for Unregister:
(1) token.CanBeCancelled == false. This will return false from Unregister.
(2) Token is cancelled before registration. This will return false from Unregister.
(3) Token is cancellable, but not cancelled before registration. This will return true if no cancellation occurs, and false if cancellation does occur.

So, it seems like we can deterministically say:
- If Unregister returns false, and token.CanBeCancelled, then the cancellation occurred.
- If Unregister returns true, or !token.CanBeCancelled, then cancellation did not occur.

Does that sound right?

>So, it seems like we can deterministically say:
>
> - If Unregister returns false, and token.CanBeCancelled, then the cancellation occurred.
> - If Unregister returns true, or !token.CanBeCancelled, then cancellation did not occur.

As I see it, doing the above **without any lock** can lead to an inconsistent shared state or a race condition because we will read `token.CanBeCanceled` and assign `_registration` in `RegisterCancellation`, but call `Unregister` in `UnregisterCancellation` or `Dispose` some time later. In the meanwhile, another thread could have changed either the stored `token.CanBeCanceled` or `_registration` .

Or, are you suggesting to get lock back here?

`token.CanBeCanceled` shouldn't ever change (at least, not until the token changes).

`_registration` should only be changed after a Reset, if I'm understanding this correctly. 

It does seem like there's a race here, but it also seems like the race already exists in the current code, if I'm understanding it correctly.
I mean that token itself is being changing each time `ResetForAwait` is called.
Actually, I don't think there's a race in the current code, because all of the manipulation of CreditWaiter is done under the Http2Stream lock.

Currently, this PR prevents a race by using compare-and-set in `ReserveCompletion`, though I just realized that setting `_completionReserved = 0` in `ResetForAwait` needs to be done through Interlocked as well.

>Actually, I don't think there's a race in the current code, because all of the manipulation of CreditWaiter is done under the Http2Stream lock.

Hmm, yes - it seems to be a good point.

>  I just realized that setting _completionReserved = 0 in ResetForAwait needs to be done through Interlocked as well.

It shouldn't. ResetForAwait is only called when ownership is well defined by construction. What path do you see where it's a problem?

> It shouldn't. ResetForAwait is only called when ownership is well defined by construction. What path do you see where it's a problem?

I'm concerned whether the `Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _completionReserved, 1, 0)` always see the latest value of `_completionReserved` set in `ResetForAwait` or there is a chance for it to see a stale data.

> always see the latest value of _completionReserved set in ResetForAwait

ResetForAwait is invoked when there is no concurrent use of the data. After this write, this thread is either the one to access the state, incurs the necessary fences to ensure the state is published and observed, and/or does something that queues the concurrent work that'll eventually read it leading to the relevant fences being in place. It's the same reason code like `int a = 42; Task.Run(() => Console.WriteLine(a));` will always print out 42 rather than 0. If that was broken here, it wouldn't just be _completionReserved that was the problem, but all of the rest of the state being updated in ResetForAwait as well.
@geoffkizer, I *think* that works.  As I noted earlier, "Potentially, but it'd require some more effort and storing more state".  But, since it seems important to you :), I'll give it a go.
Feedback addressed. I don't plan to add to httpstress in this PR. We should spend some time separately augmenting it to be able to handle more cases.

@stephentoub It seems all comments are now resolved and all checks are green. So can I merge it into the master?

issue_context.title: HTTP2: Hang when concurrent calls with cancellation
issue_context.body:
<!--This is just a template - feel free to delete any and all of it and replace as appropriate.-->

### Description

Grpc.Net.Client (which uses HttpClient internally) is hanging when there are 20 concurrent calls with cancellation happening in a loop.

Repo: [repos.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/files/4944674/repos.zip)

1. Extract to directory
2. dotnet run -p GrpcService28
3. dotnet run -p ConsoleApp50
4. ConsoleApp will throw timeout exceptions after a few hundred/thousand iterations.

Changing ConsoleApp50 target framework from net5.0 to netcoreapp3.1 fixes the timeout exceptions.

Normally I'd attempt to remove Grpc.Net.Client library from the repo, but in this case the gRPC call is using a number of fairly advanced features (bidi streaming, cancellation) so I have left it in.

What console app is doing (20 parallel threads on one HTTP/2 connection):

1. Starting bidi streaming call, `client.EchoAllData(cancellationToken: cts.Token, headers: headers)`
2. Waiting for the call response headers from server, `await call.ResponseHeadersAsync.DefaultTimeout();`
3. Writing 64kb message, `await call.RequestStream.WriteAsync(...)` **<- this is where the hang happens**
4. Cancelling call, `cts.Cancel();`
5. Go to 1

### Configuration

Using nightly SDK: 5.0.100-rc.1.20367.2

### Regression?

Yes, this worked in netcoreapp3.1

It seems I found the root cause. There is a deadlock between processing WindowUpdateFrame and cancelling Http2Stream.

1. `Http2Stream.SendDataAsync` calls `Http2Connection.SendStreamDataAsync` passing `_requestBodyCancellationSource.Token` to cancel sending request body if a need arises later.
2. `Http2Connection.SendStreamDataAsync` tries to acquire connection window credit of the frame's size to send a next chunk of data. To do that, it calls `await _connectionWindow.RequestCreditAsync(frameSize, cancellationToken)` where `cancellationToken` is the token supplied by `Http2Stream` at the step 1.
3. In case no credit is available, `CreditManager.RequestCreditAsync` creates `CancelableCreditWaiter` passing `this` (the reference to the current `CreditManager` instance) as SyncObject and still the same `cancellationToken` to the constructor.
4. `CancelableCreditWaiter` registers a callback on that `cancellationToken` and stores the `CancellationTokenRegistration` in `_registration`. The first thing the callback will do is to acquire lock on `_syncObject` that points to `CreditManager` from the step 3.
5. Some time later. `GrpcCall<T>.CancelCall` disposes `HttpResponseMessage` that subsequently disposes `HttpConnectionResponseContent` where `Http2Stream.Cancel` gets called at some point.
6. `Http2Stream.Cancel` checks whether a request is still in progress and since it is so, it tries to cancel the request by calling `requestBodyCancellationSource?.Cancel()`.
7. `requestBodyCancellationSource` calls the `CancelableCreditWaiter`'s cancellation callback registered at step 4 that tries **to lock on `_syncObejct` which still points to `_connectionWindow`** from step 2. However, the lock happens to be already taken, so **it waits.**
8. In parallel with steps 5-7, `Http2Connection.ProcessIncomingFramesAsync` receives a `WindowUpdate` frame and calls `ProcessWindowUpdateFrame`.
9. `ProcessWindowUpdateFrame` updates connection window credits by calling `_connectionWindow.AdjustCredit(amount)`. `_connectionWindow` is the same `CreditManager` on which we called `RequestCreditAsync` at the step 2 and which passed itself (`this`) as `_syncObject` to `CancelableCreditWaiter`.
10. **`CreditManager.AdjustCredit` locks on itself (`this`)** and calls `waiter.Dispose()` where `waiter` is `CancelableCreditWaiter` from step 4 with a cancellation callback.
11. `CancelableCreditWaiter.Dispose` eventually calls `_registration.Dispose`. `_registration` was assigned to at step 4 and is linked to request cancellation token belonging to `_requestBodyCancellationSource` from step 1.
12. `_registration.Dispose` eventually calls `CancellationTokenSource.WaitForCallbackToComplete` that start waiting for an executing cancellation callback to complete by looping over `SpinLock` with `while (ExecutingCallback == id)`. However, the callback being executed right now is the one where **thread closing `Http2Stream` got blocked at step 7** while waiting for a lock on the same `_connectionWindow` object as the one **we locked on at step 10**.
13. **Deadlock!**
